Dathan
dā'than
n. (a Reubenite who joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and was swallowed alive by the earth)
From Hebrew Dathan, of uncertain derivation. He is never named apart from his brother Abiram; the two are the Reubenite half of a rebellion whose other half was Levitical.

Biblical Definition

Dathan son of Eliab was a Reubenite, and with his brother Abiram he joined the conspiracy of Korah the Levite against Moses and Aaron (Num 16:1). The alliance is instructive: Korah wanted the priesthood, the Reubenites wanted the civil leadership, and the two grievances found each other. Summoned to answer, they refused with contempt: “And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab: which said, We will not come up” (Num 16:12), and they went on to accuse Moses of dragging Israel out of a land flowing with milk and honey — meaning Egypt — to kill them in the wilderness. Judgment came on their own doorsteps. “Dathan and Abiram came out, and stood in the door of their tents, and their wives, and their sons, and their little children” (Num 16:27), and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them and their households. Numbers records the whole thing again in the second census as a warning to a new generation: “This is that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the LORD” (Num 26:9). That last clause is the doctrine of the passage. To strive against God's appointed servants was, in the end, to strive against the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Dathan; in sacred history he is a Reubenite who conspired with Korah against Moses, and was swallowed up by the earth.

expand to see more

DATHAN, n. The son of Eliab, of the tribe of Reuben.

With his brother Abiram he joined Korah the Levite in rebellion against Moses and Aaron.

Being summoned, he refused to come up, and reproached Moses concerning the land of Egypt.

The earth opened her mouth and swallowed him, with his household and his goods.

Moses recites the judgment in Deuteronomy as a warning to Israel.

Key Scripture

Num 16:1 — "Now Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men:"

Num 16:12 — "And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab: which said, We will not come up:"

Num 16:27 — "So they gat up from the tabernacle of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, on every side: and Dathan and Abiram came out, and stood in the door of their tents, and their wives, and their sons, and their little children."

Num 26:9 — "And the sons of Eliab; Nemuel, and Dathan, and Abiram. This is that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the LORD:"

Modern Corruption

The rebellion is recast as a democratic protest against clerical privilege, and the judgment as an authoritarian atrocity — a reading that has to ignore what the rebels actually said and whom Numbers says they were striving against.

expand to see more

Korah's slogan sounds admirable in translation: all the congregation are holy, every one of them, wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the LORD? Modern readings take it at face value and make Moses the villain of an egalitarian parable. Two things are fatal to that reading. First, Moses did not lift himself up; God called him from a bush he ran away from, and Numbers calls him the meekest man on the face of the earth. Second, Numbers itself supplies the interpretation: they “strove against the LORD”. Where God has appointed an office, contempt for the office is contempt for the One who gave it. Jude places this episode among his three examples of apostasy — “perished in the gainsaying of Core” (Jud 1:11).

The second corruption is the flinching at the judgment, particularly at the little children standing in the tent doors. The dictionary does not soften it and does not pretend the passage is comfortable. It observes what Scripture observes: that God is the Judge of all the earth and shall do right (Gen 18:25); that households in the ancient covenant order stood or fell with their heads, which is a solemn argument for the weight of a father's choices rather than an argument against God; and that the sons of Korah did not die (Num 26:11), and afterward wrote psalms. Mercy ran even through that ground. Judgment fell where it was earned, and a line was spared where God chose to spare it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Dathan (H1885), Dathan; Qorach (H7141), Korah; matseh, strife; nātsāh (H5327), to strive, contend; She'ol (H7585), the pit, the grave.

expand to see more

Hebrew Dathan (H1885) — Dathan; a Reubenite, son of Eliab.

Hebrew Qorach (H7141) — Korah; the Levite whose priestly ambition led the conspiracy.

Hebrew natsah (H5327) — to strive, contend, quarrel; the verb of Num 26:9.

Hebrew She'ol (H7585) — the grave, the pit; whither they went down alive.

Hebrew 'edah (H5712) — congregation, assembly; the body they claimed to speak for.

Usage

"“We will not come up” — four words that settled a man's case."

"“Which strove against Moses and against Aaron… when they strove against the LORD” — the inspired reading of the quarrel."

"“Stood in the door of their tents” — defiance to the last hour."
